===Etymology 1===
{{etymon|en|id=approach|:inh|enm:comen|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|comen}}, {{m|enm|cumen}}, from {{inh|en|ang|cuman}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*kweman}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*kwemaną|t=to come}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*gʷémt|t=to step; to arrive}}, from {{m|ine-pro|*gʷem-|t=to come, step}}.
{{col-top|2|cog}}
Cognate from Proto-Germanic with {{cog|sco|cum|t=to come}}, {{cog|yol|come}}, {{m|yol|coome}}, {{m|yol|cum|t=to come}}, {{cog|frr|kaame}}, {{m|frr|kame}}, {{m|frr|keem}}, {{m|frr|kem}}, {{m|frr|kum}}, {{m|frr|kååme}}, {{m|frr|käme|t=to come}}, {{cog|stq|kume}}, {{m|stq|kuume|t=to come}}, {{cog|fy|komme|t=to come}}, {{cog|gsw|cha}}, {{m|gsw|cheemen}}, {{m|gsw|cheme}}, {{m|gsw|cho}}, {{m|gsw|chomu}}, {{m|gsw|chéeme|t=to come}}, {{cog|bar|ckeman}}, {{m|bar|kemma}}, {{m|bar|kemman}}, {{m|bar|khemen}}, {{m|bar|kumma}}, {{m|bar|kumman}}, {{m|bar|kèmmin|t=to come}}, {{cog|gmw-cfr|komme}}, {{m|gmw-cfr|kunn}}, {{m|gmw-cfr|kumme|t=to come}}, {{cog|cim|ken}}, {{m|cim|khemmen}}, {{m|cim|khèmman|t=to come}}, {{cog|nl|komen}}, {{m|nl|kommen|t=to come}}, {{cog|nds-nl|kåmen|t=to come}}, {{cog|de,lb|kommen|t=to come}}, {{cog|nds|kamen}}, {{m|nds|kuemen|t=to come}}, {{cog|mhn|kemmen|t=to come}}, {{cog|yi|קימען }}, {{m|yi|קומען|t=to come}}, {{cog|da,nb|komme|t=to come}}, {{cog|ovd|kumå|t=to come}}, {{cog|fo,is|koma|t=to come; to arrive}}, {{cog|gmq-jmk|kuma|t=to come}}, {{cog|nn|koma}}, {{m|nn|komma}}, {{m|nn|komme}}, {{m|nn|kåmmå}}, {{m|nn|kåmå|t=to come}}, {{cog|sv|komma|t=to come}}, {{cog|gme-cgo|kommen|t=to come}}, {{cog|got|𐌵𐌹𐌼𐌰𐌽|t=to come}}.

====Verb====
{{en-verb|come<,,came:~[dialectal],~:came[dialectal]:~n>}}

# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[move]] [[near]]er to the point of [[perspective]].
#: {{ux|en|She’ll be '''coming''' round the mountain when she '''comes''' the wrong way {{...}}}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Merry Wives|act=II|scene=i|passage=Look, who '''comes''' yonder?}}
#* {{RQ:Tennyson Idylls|page=253|passage=Yet think not that I '''come''' to urge thy crimes, / I did not '''come''' to curse thee, Guinevere, {{...}}}}
## To move toward the speaker.
##: {{ux|en|I called the dog, but she wouldn't '''come'''.}}
##: {{ux|en|Stop dawdling and '''come''' here!}}
##: {{ux|en|'''Come''' one, '''come''' all. Step right up!}} 
## To move toward the listener.
##: {{ux|en|Hold on, I'll '''come''' in a second.}}
##: {{ux|en|You should ask the doctor to '''come''' to your house.}}
## To move toward the object that is the [[w:Focus (linguistics)|focus]] of the sentence.
##: {{ux|en|No-one can find Bertie Wooster when his aunts '''come''' to visit.}}
##: {{ux|en|Hundreds of thousands of people '''come''' to Disneyland every year.}}
## {{lb|en|in subordinate clauses and gerunds}} To move toward the [[w:Agent (grammar)|agent]] or subject of the main clause.
##: {{ux|en|King Cnut couldn't stop the tide '''coming'''.}}
##: {{ux|en|He threw the boomerang, which '''came''' right back to him.}}
## To move toward an unstated agent.
##: {{ux|en|The butler should '''come''' when called.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[arrive]].
#* {{RQ:Pepys Diary|volume=VI|date=13 June 1667|page=364|passage=Late at night '''comes''' Mr. Hudson, the cooper, my neighbour, and tells me that he '''come''' from Chatham this evening at five o'clock, and saw this afternoon "The Royal James," "Oake," and "London," burnt by the enemy with their fire-ships: {{...}}|footer=This passage uses the [[historical present]] [[tense]].}}
#* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=5|passage=Then '''came''' a maid with hand-bag and shawls, and after her a tall young lady. She stood for a moment holding her skirt above the grimy steps,{{...}}, and the light of the reflector fell full upon her.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|date=11 January 2013|origyear=1997|author=David Bell; Gill Valentine|publisher=Routledge|title=Consuming Geographies: We Are Where We Eat|isbn=9781442432949|page=140|url=https://books.google.co.nz/books?id=cM70Uhk0r88C|passage=So I'd have ate{{sic}} when me Dad had ate, sort of thing, I think, you know when he '''come''' home from work, I'd have waited for him, I wouldn't have said I wanted mine at four o'clock{{...}}}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[appear]]; to [[manifest]] itself; to cause a reaction by manifesting.
#: {{ux|en|The pain in his leg '''comes''' and goes.}}
#: {{ux|en|The news '''came''' as a shock.}}
#*{{quote-text|en|title=Diary|author={{w|Lou Sullivan}}|date=4 Jan 1965|text=Kathy and I had a teen-age girl to girl talk, about boys, John, and understanding Mom. I was gonna tell her about Phil but I held my mouth till tears '''came'''.}}
# {{lb|en|with an infinitive}} To [[begin]] (to have an opinion or feeling).
#: {{ux|en|We '''came''' to believe that he was not so innocent after all.}}
#: {{ux|en|She '''came''' to think of that country as her home.}}
#* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=3|passage=Now all this was very fine, but not at all in keeping with the Celebrity's character as I had '''come''' to conceive it. The idea that adulation ever cloyed on him was ludicrous in itself. In fact I thought the whole story fishy, and '''came''' very near to saying so.}}
# {{lb|en|with an infinitive}} To [[do]] something [[by chance]] or [[unintentionally]].
#: {{ux|en|Could you tell me how the document '''came''' to be discovered?}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To take a position relative to something else in a [[sequence]].
#: {{ux|en|Which letter '''comes''' before Y?   Winter '''comes''' after autumn.}}
# {{senseid|en|orgasm}}{{lb|en|intransitive|often vulgar|slang}} To achieve [[orgasm]]; to [[cum #Verb|cum]]; to [[ejaculate]].
#: {{ux|en|She '''came''' after a few minutes.}}
#: {{ux|en|'''Come''' in me!}}
#* {{RQ:Hollinghurst Line|chapter=2|passage=Nick was more and more seriously absorbed, but then just before he '''came''' he had a brief vision of himself, as if the trees and bushes had rolled away and all the lights of London shone in on him: little Nick Guest from Barwick, Don and Dot Guest's boy, fucking a stranger in a Notting Hill garden at night.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2008|author=w:Philip Roth|title={{w|Indignation (novel)|Indignation}}|passage= The sheer unimaginableness of '''coming''' into her mouth — of '''coming''' into anything other than the air or a tissue or a dirty sock — was an allurement too stupendous for a novice to forswear.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|of milk}} To become [[butter]] by being [[churned]].
#* {{RQ:Butler Hudibras|year=1905|passage=when butter does refuse to '''come'''}}
# {{lb|en|copulative|figuratively}} To [[approach]] or [[reach]] a state of being or accomplishment.
#: {{ux|en|They '''came''' very close to leaving on time.   His test scores '''came''' close to perfect.}}
#: {{ux|en|One of the screws '''came''' loose, and the skateboard fell apart.}}

#: {{ux|en|He '''came''' to SF literature a confirmed technophile, and nothing made him happier than to read a manuscript thick with imaginary gizmos and whatzits.}}

"Drat the boy," cried the old lady, wrathfully.  "Stand still, do!  Will he ever '''come''' clean?"|url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Poster/tWOq9AcelioC?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PT7&printsec=frontcover|title=The Poster|section=Notable Poster Illustrations|page=17|publisher=Poster Advertising Association}}

#: {{ux|en|He's as tough as they '''come'''.}}
#: {{ux|en|Our milkshakes '''come''' in vanilla, strawberry and chocolate flavours.}}
#: {{ux|en|A new sports car doesn't '''come''' cheap.}}
# {{lb|en|slang}} To carry through; to succeed in.
#: {{ux|en|You can't '''come''' any tricks here.}}

#: {{syn|en|come about|occur|take place}}
#: {{ux|en|This kind of accident '''comes''' when you are careless.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=2014-06-14|volume=411|issue=8891|magazine=w:The Economist
|title=[http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21604091-it-possible-sniff-out-problems-sewer-pipes-they-happen-its-gas It's a gas]
|passage=But out of sight is out of mind. And that{{...}}means that many old sewers have been neglected and are in dire need of repair. If that repair does not '''come''' in time, the result is noxious and potentially hazardous.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|with ''from'' or sometimes ''of''}} To have as an [[origin]], [[originate]].
## To have a certain [[social]] [[background]].
##* {{quote-book|en|year=2011|author=Kate Gramich|title=Kate Roberts|publisher=University of Wales Press|isbn=9780708323380|chapter=3|page={{gbooks|vE2uBwAAQBAJ|46|came}}
|passage=While Kate Roberts '''came''' from a poor background and, later in life, in the post-Second World War period suffered from severe money shortages, in the early 1930s, she and her husband must have counted themselves relatively well off, particularly in comparison with their neighbours in Tonypandy.}}
## To be or have been a resident or native.
##: {{ux|en|Where did you '''come''' from?}}
## To have been brought up by or employed by.
##: {{ux|en|She '''comes''' from a good family.}}
##: {{ux|en|He '''comes''' from a disreputable legal firm.}}
## To [[begin]] (at a certain location); to [[radiate]] or [[stem]] (from).
##: {{ux|en|The river '''comes''' from Bear Lake.}}
##: {{ux|en|Where does this road '''come''' from?}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|of ''grain''}} To [[germinate]].
# {{lb|en|transitive|informal}} To [[pretend]] to be; to behave in the manner of; to assume the [[role]] of.
#: {{ux|en|Don’t '''come''' the innocent victim. We all know who’s to blame here.}}
#* {{RQ:Dickens Oliver Twist|passage=“Hush! hush! Mr. Sikes,” said the Jew, trembling; “don’t speak so loud!” / “None of your mistering,” replied the ruffian; “you always mean mischief when you '''come''' that. You know my name: out with it! I shan’t disgrace it when the time comes.”}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1950|author=Norman Lindsay|authorlink=Norman Lindsay|title={{w|Dust or Polish?}}|publisher=Angus and Robertson|location=Sydney|page=157|passage=Ponds drew a chair to the table and seated himself and poured Mrs Dibble a gin, saying solemnly, "Now then, Mrs Dibble, what's it all about?" "I'm upholding my rights agen that woman that's been '''coming''' the high and mighty over me like I ain't got the right to say a word in me own business."}}

=====Usage notes=====
* In its general sense, ''come'' specifically marks motion {{l|en|towards}} the [[w:Deixis|deictic]] centre, (whether explicitly stated or not). Its counterpart, usually referring to motion away from or not involving the deictic centre, is {{m|en|go}}. For example, the sentence "Come to the tree" implies contextually that the speaker is already at the tree — "Go to the tree" often implies that the speaker is elsewhere. Either the speaker or the listener can be the deictic centre — the sentences "I will go to you" and "I will come to you" are both valid, depending on the exact nuances of the context. When there is no clear speaker or listener, the deictic centre is usually the focus of the sentence or the topic of the piece of writing. "Millions of people '''came''' to America from Europe" would be used in an article about America, but "Millions of people '''went''' to America from Europe" would be used in an article about Europe.

* When used with adverbs of location, ''come'' is usually paired with {{m|en|here}} or {{m|en|hither}}. In interrogatives, ''come'' usually indicates a question about source — "Where are you coming from?" — while ''go'' indicates a question about destination — "Where are you going?" or "Where are you going to?"

* A few old texts use {{m|en|comen}} as the past participle. Also, in some dialects, like rural Scots and rural Midlands dialects, the form {{m|en|comen}} is still occasionally in use, so phrases like the following can still be encountered there — ''Sa thoo bist comen heyr to nim min 'orse frae mee, then?'' {{IPAchar|[sä ðuː bɪst cʊmn̩ hiər tə nɪm miːn ɔːrs frə miː {{!}} d̪ɛn]}} (so you have come here to steal my horse from me, then?).

* Formerly the verb {{m|en|be}} was used as the auxiliary instead of {{m|en|have}}, for example, ''Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and '''are''' come to worship him.''

* The collocations {{m|en|come with}} and {{m|en|come along}} mean {{m|en|accompany}}, used as "Do you want to come with me?" and "Do you want to come along?" In the Midwestern American dialect, "come with" can occur without a following object, as in "Do you want to come with?" In this dialect, "with" can also be used in this way with some other verbs, such as "take with". Examples of this may be found in plays by Chicagoan {{w|David Mamet}}, such as ''{{w|American Buffalo}}.''<ref>[http://positiveanymore.blogspot.com/2006/04/chicago-dialect.html Chicago Dialect]</ref> This objectless use is not permissible in other dialects.

* The meaning in the sense of ''to ejaculate'' or ''orgasm'' is often considered vulgar slang. Many style guides and editors recommend the spelling ''come'' for verb uses while strictly allowing the spelling {{m|en|cum}} for the noun. Both spellings are sometimes found in either the noun or verb sense, however. Others prefer to distinguish in formality, using ''come'' for any formal usage and ''cum'' only in slang, erotic or pornographic contexts.<ref>[http://www.glossophilia.org/?p=4925 Glossophilia]</ref>

=====Usage notes=====
* The meaning of ''semen or female ejaculatory discharge'' is considered vulgar slang. Many style guides and editors recommend the spelling ''come'' for verb uses while strictly allowing the spelling {{m|en|cum}} for the noun. Both spellings are sometimes found in either the noun or verb sense, however. Others prefer to distinguish in formality, using ''come'' for any formal usage and ''cum'' only in slang, erotic or pornographic contexts.<ref>[http://www.glossophilia.org/?p=4925 Glossophilia]</ref>
